newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan minister starts Africa tour to secure ties.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan minister starts Africa tour to secure ties.

text.p: Taiwan Foreign Minister John Chang left for Africa on Sunday for a seven-nation tour, hoping to shore up diplomatic ties after Pretoria's announcement it is to abandon Taipei and open relations with Beijing.
On the same day, Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, who doubles as China's vice-premier, is also scheduled to visit five other nations in the African continent to promote ties.
"It's very apparant that the diplomatic war across the Taiwan Strait is now in the ascendant in Africa," Taiwan's state-run Central News Agency reported.
Chang will visit South Africa, Swaziland, Malawi, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Bissau, Gambia and Senegal before his scheduled return to Taiwan on February 2.

"As long as we are firm in our stance and have a clear direction, the Republic of China will have more friends on the international stage and receive more recognition and support," Chang said before boarding at Taipei's international airport.
Africa has been a main battlefield for the decades-old diplomatic war between Taiwan and China -- political rivals since a civil war separated them in 1949.
Taiwan, internationally isolated by China, has been struggling to win foreign ties with its strong economic muscle while China also uses financial aid to lure poor states.
South Africa, the biggest of Taiwan's only 30 diplomatic allies, announced in late 1996 that it would switch recognition to Beijing from Taipei by the end of 1997.
Analysts have warned of a possible "domino effect" following Pretoria's announcement and Chang's trip is clearly a move to control possible diplomatic damage.

Before South Africa, Niger switched ties to Communist China from Nationalist Taiwan in August 1996, cutting the number of the island's allies, mostly under-developed states in Africa and central America, to 30 from 31.

Despite Pretoria's decision, Taiwan has said it hopes to maintain the highest level of relations with South Africa after their formal diplomatic ties were severed. Its aid projects there would depend on the level of new relations.

The diplomatic war intensified on Friday when China vetoed a resolution to send 155 United Nations peacekeepers to Guatemala, which recognises Taipei, because of the Central American country's "erroneous position" in supporting Taiwan.
It was the first time Beijing had used its veto power in nearly 24 years.
China inists that Taiwan is a Chinese province not entitled to foreign recognition and demands countries that desire ties with China sever ties with Taiwan first.
Both governments in Taipei and Beijing say they want reunification, but under very different terms.
Taiwan insists it has the right to develop its own foreign relations before reunification can be realised.
Both Taiwan and China have been assisting poor African states and blasted each other for playing "money politics" in Africa.
